title: School Notebooks 5-pack

drivers.name: Price Increase to $9.03
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks at $9.03: sales of 10 and 7 units (vs baseline 7.6). Noise-adjusted estimate of price effect is x0.95. Shrink due to limited data and no prior higher price points.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 7.6. No events are scheduled. The price increased by 2.3% to $9.03. Past price hikes to $9.03 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw sales drop to 10 and 7 units, respectively—below baseline. The noise-adjusted effect of a $9.03 price point is x0.95 vs baseline (average of 10/7 = 1.43, but baseline is 7.6, so 10/7.6 ≈ 1.32, 7/7.6 ≈ 0.92; mean ~1.12, but noise-adjusted toward 1.0). Given only two data points and no prior price increases at this level, shrink to x0.95. No promotion, season, or event. The classical model's 1.00 is a starting point but ignores price impact. Confidence is medium due to limited data.

brief:
PRODUCT: School Notebooks 5-pack | category Office | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 (6 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 9.03 (+2.3% vs regular price 8.83)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 7.6 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 37.9 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 24.5

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-64% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
